extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of literary criticism (particularly 19th-century European poetry)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-evaluation guidance for 19th-century poetry and prose: identifies aesthetic, moral, cultural, and editorial qualities by which poets (e.g., Heine, Byron, Shelley) and collections (e.g., Abbé Migne) are to be judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of modern ideas to life
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that apply modern ideas to life belong to the main current of modern literature; those that do not 'do not apply modern ideas to life; they constitute... minor currents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central test of literary greatness in the modern epoch is whether a writer freely applies contemporary (nineteenth-century) ideas to life. Examples: Shakespeare/Goethe/Heine apply modern ideas and are in the main current; Wordsworth/Scott/Keats and much popular work that avoid modern ideas constitute 'minor currents.' Byron and Shelley attempted but were resisted and thus failed to fully enter the main stream.

rubrics_metrics.name: National intellectual environment as support
rubrics_metrics.description: Great literature is often 'powerfully upheld by the intellectual life of [its] nation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nation's intellectual climate and sympathetic audiences enable writers to develop and sustain modern literary movements; lack of such support (e.g., English middle-class Puritanism for Byron/Shelley) can stifle otherwise gifted writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute freedom; rejection of stock classicism and romanticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Modernism involves 'absolute freedom, [an] utter rejection of stock classicism and stock romanticism' and bringing things under the nineteenth-century point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued modern writing abandons clichéd classical or romantic formulas and reframes subjects through contemporary sensibilities and critical perspective; Heine exemplifies this by combining French wit with German culture while rejecting stale modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness, lightness, and freedom combined with power of feeling and width of range
rubrics_metrics.description: Heine's characteristics: 'wonderful clearness, lightness, and freedom, united with such power of feeling, and width of range.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry that balances lucidity and formal ease with genuine feeling and wide thematic range is especially prized. The critic cites specific witty anecdotes and diverse poetic subjects as evidence of this prized balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of popular ballad-form with rapidity and grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Heine 'chiefly uses a form of old German popular poetry, a ballad-form which has more rapidity and grace than any ballad-form of ours.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of a traditional popular form can be an asset when employed with lightness and fullness; such forms can combine grace and rapid movement with pathos and old-world charm, making them effective vehicles for modern content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blending French modernism and German sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: In Heine's poetry 'one perpetually blends the impression of French modernism and clearness, with that of German sentiment and fulness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The stylistic synthesis of different national traits (e.g., French clarity and German fulness) is a notable criterion for assessing tonal richness and originality; the blend should be perceptible in both form and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of voice and remaining of one's own century
rubrics_metrics.description: Heine 'never does...attempt to be schön objektiv... he always remains Heinrich Heine, a son of the nineteenth century.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good modern writer maintains an authentic contemporary voice rather than impersonating earlier epochs (Middle-Age knights, old Hebrews, etc.). Authenticity of perspective—being unmistakably of one's age—is a virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form as expression of cultural spirits (Greek beauty vs Hebrew sublimity)
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'perfection of literary form, by his love of clearness, by his love of beauty, Heine is Greek; by his intensity... he is Hebrew.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how cultural influences shape a poet's aims: beauty (Greek) tends toward formal perfection and clarity; sublimity (Hebrew) tends toward intensity and transcendence. The interaction of these impulses is a key measure of poetic achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit and irony as markers of modern mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Heine's wit and irony—illustrated by anecdotes (the French abbé, Professor Saalfeld, the national-wife comparison)—display 'incomparable' and 'truly modern' mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharp, delicate, and inventive wit (including ironic turns that may end in grim innuendo) is a hallmark of modern literary skill; use of irony to expose social or national traits is commended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical rhythm, musicality, and suitability of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between awkward verse by some French writers in German and Heine's successful Lieder: 'what a blessing to arrive at rhythms like—' (quoted English/German lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical rhythm and natural idiomatic phrasing are essential; a poet who finds his 'freest and most perfect expression' in verse (as Heine does) exemplifies the importance of fitting rhythm and language. Translators may only reproduce part of this quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melancholy/plaintive note and expression of exile
rubrics_metrics.description: Heine's 'sweetest note' is plaintive melancholy, evident in his late 'mattress-grave' poems where he longs for Germany and expresses exile and infirmity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to convey elegiac, plaintive feelings—exile, homesickness, mortal frailty—with sincerity and evocative detail is a significant poetic virtue, adding depth to a body of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral balance, self-respect, and dignity of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Great interpreters of the modern world require an 'immense' moral deliverance; Heine (and Byron) show 'a deficiency in self-respect, in true dignity of character' and thus produce 'half-results.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond intellectual or formal gifts, moral balance and nobility of soul are judged necessary for a poet to be an 'adequate interpreter' of his age. Lack of moral balance or generosity diminishes ultimate greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abundance/richness of archival or collected material as value
rubrics_metrics.description: Collections like Abbé Migne's 'embrace the whole range of human interests... like one of the great Middle-Age Cathedrals, it is in itself a study for a life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large compilations that gather diverse religious, historical, and cultural materials are valuable research resources; their breadth and sheer suggestiveness make them indispensable despite editorial defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial quality vs quantity in compilations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Do not seek in it splendour of form, perfection of editing; its paper is common, its type ugly, its editing indifferent... The greatest... crowd of misprints I ever met.' Quantity rather than quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing large collections, weigh breadth and accessibility against sloppy editing and production; expect misprints and careless editing in massive compilations and account for them in critical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of impartiality and the reader's need to do criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Do not seek in it impartiality, the critical spirit; in reading it you must do the criticism for yourself; it loves criticism as little as the world loves it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compilations and doctrinal works may be partisan and present one-sided 'pros' for their position. The competent reader must apply critical judgment rather than accept the compiler's slant; awareness of bias is a necessary evaluative practice.
